examGuide.title: Mental model and derivation
examGuide.body:
Counting sort uses key-range size k and costs Θ(n+k). LSD radix sorting uses stable digit passes so a later significant digit does not destroy previous ordering among ties. Digit width trades alphabet size against pass count. Key width and sign handling are algorithm assumptions, not free constants. These methods can beat comparison bounds only by exploiting representation and bounded ranges.

**Key relationship:** Counting sort: Θ(n+k); radix with d digits and base b: Θ(d(n+b))

examGuide.title: A repeatable solving procedure
examGuide.body:
1. Specify key range and width.
2. Choose stable digit processing.
3. Count passes times per-pass work.

examGuide.title: Approach the exam question
examGuide.body: Counting sort takes Θ(n+k) for range k. LSD radix sorting requires a stable digit sort so later passes preserve earlier digit ordering. Choose digit width by balancing pass count with per-pass alphabet size. Key width is part of the assumptions, not always a hidden constant.

examGuide.title: Worked problem
examGuide.body:
How many base-16 LSD radix passes are needed for unsigned 20-bit keys?

**Answer: 5.** A hexadecimal digit contains four bits. Required passes=ceil(20/4)=5. Leading zero digits can be included without changing the final order.

examGuide.title: Conditions and edge cases
examGuide.body:
Signed keys require a sign-handling convention. An unstable per-digit sort can invalidate LSD radix sorting.

Counting sort is not efficient when the key range is enormous compared with n.

examGuide.title: Worked question patterns
examGuide.body:
#### Pattern 1 · MCQ

LSD radix sorting requires each digit pass to be:

- **A.** Comparison-based
- **B.** Unstable
- **C.** Stable
- **D.** Descending only

**Answer: C.** Stability preserves the less-significant-digit order when current digits tie.

#### Pattern 2 · MSQ

Choose true statements.

- **A.** Counting sort depends on key range
- **B.** Radix passes depend on digit width
- **C.** All integer sorting is Θ(n) regardless of key width
- **D.** Noncomparison methods use assumptions beyond comparisons

**Answer: A, B, D.** Unbounded representation/range costs prevent a universal linear-time claim.

#### Pattern 3 · NAT

Number of base-256 passes for unsigned 32-bit keys?



**Answer: 4.** Each base-256 digit holds eight bits; 32/8=4 passes.
